hints: Line up the two DNA coding strands letter by letter and find the single base that is different in HbS compared to HbA.
Remember how that changed DNA triplet will be transcribed into a changed mRNA codon, and then how an mRNA codon pairs by hydrogen bonds with a complementary tRNA anticodon during translation.
walkthrough:
**Spot the exact mutation**

Look closely at the two coding strands side by side. Everything is identical except one base.

$$HbA: ...CCT GAG GAG...$$
$$HbS: ...CCT GTG GAG...$$
This is a single base substitution, A to T in the coding strand. It changes only one triplet from GAG to GTG.

**Transcribe to mRNA**

During transcription the template is used to build a complementary mRNA, so the altered DNA triplet leads to an altered mRNA codon.
In this example the HbS mRNA contains the altered codon CAC where HbA had CUC. Only this one codon is changed, the rest of the message stays the same.

**Pair codon with anticodon in translation**

In translation, each mRNA codon hydrogen bonds to a complementary tRNA anticodon by specific base pairing, C with G and A with U.
The altered CAC codon will therefore pair with a tRNA carrying the complementary anticodon GUG, bringing a different amino acid, valine instead of glutamic acid, into the beta-globin chain.

options.A: Correct. The altered mRNA codon pairs complementarily with a tRNA anticodon GUG by C-G, A-U and C-G hydrogen bonds, delivering the new amino acid.
options.B: False. This is a substitution, not a deletion or insertion, so there is no frameshift. Only the one amino acid at that position changes.
options.C: False. mRNA never contains the base T, it contains U. The codons would be written with U, not CTC and CAC as DNA triplets.
options.D: False. The mutation does not create a stop codon. The ribosome can continue translation and simply inserts valine, making a full length polypeptide.
